entry: Northwest Semitic supreme deity of the ancient Canaanite religion. The word *el* means "god" or "deity" in Semitic languages. Often described as the father of the gods and the creator of humanity, El presided over a council of gods. In Ugaritic and Levantine mythology he fathered [[Baal]] and other major deities. In Israelite religion, [[Yahweh]] came to absorb many of El's characteristics.

Ancient civilization centered in southwestern [[Iran]]. Elamite states were among the leading political forces of the ancient Near East, and Elam was part of the early urbanization of the region during the [[Chalcolithic|Chalcolithic period]]. Written records emerged around 3000 BC, paralleling [[Sumer|Sumerian]] history. In the Old Elamite period ([[Bronze Age|Middle Bronze Age]]), Elam consisted of kingdoms on the [[Iranian plateau]], centered at Anshan; from the mid-2nd millennium BC its center was [[Susa]], in the Khuzestan lowlands. Elamite administrative traditions became an important foundation of the later Iranian administrative system. The Achaemenid Persians conquered Elam in 539 BC.

Measure of a material's resistance to elastic (non-permanent) deformation under [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]]. It is defined as the slope of the stress–strain curve in the elastic region, so a [[Stiffness|stiffer]] material has a higher elastic modulus. Several types describe different modes of deformation. [[Young's modulus]] (E) describes tensile and compressive elasticity and is defined as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain; it is often called simply the elastic modulus. The shear modulus (G) describes deformation of shape at constant volume, and the bulk modulus (K) describes volumetric elasticity and is the inverse of compressibility. Fluids at rest cannot support shear stress, so their shear modulus is zero; moving fluids experience shear stresses that give rise to [[Viscosity|viscosity]]. Steel has a Young's modulus of around 200 GPa, while rubber's is about 0.01–0.1 GPa.

Physical property by which a body returns to its original size and shape after deformation. Studied in [[Continuum mechanics|continuum mechanics]] and [[Materials science|materials science]], elasticity is quantified in engineering by [[Elastic modulus|elastic moduli]], which relate stress to strain. Solids deform under adequate loads and recover their shape if they are elastic, in contrast to [[Plasticity (physics)|plastic]] behavior, in which the deformation is permanent. In [[Metal|metals]], the atomic lattice changes size and shape under force and returns to its lower-energy state when the force is removed; in rubbers and other [[Polymer|polymers]], elasticity arises from the stretching of polymer chains. [[Hooke's law]] states that the force needed to deform an elastic object is proportional to the distance of deformation, an ideal that most materials follow only for small deformations. The elastic limit, or yield strength, is the maximum [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]] a material can bear before plastic deformation begins.

Major river of [[Central Europe]], flowing from the [[Czech Republic]] to the [[North Sea]]. It rises in the Giant Mountains of the northern Czech Republic, flows through Bohemia and then [[Germany]], and enters the North Sea at Cuxhaven, 110 km northwest of [[Hamburg]]. Its total length is 1,094 km. Major tributaries include the Vltava, Ohře, Saale, Havel, Mulde and Schwarze Elster. The Elbe basin covers 148,268 sq km, the twelfth-largest catchment in Europe, and is inhabited by 24.4 million people. Most of the basin lies in Germany (65.5%) and the Czech Republic (33.7%). Major cities include [[Berlin]], Hamburg, [[Prague]] and [[Dresden]]. Floods have repeatedly affected the river; a 2002 flood caused over 11 billion euros in damage in Germany.

American diplomat and activist. Longest-serving First Lady of the United States, during the presidency of her husband, [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]], from 1933 to 1945. She largely redefined the role through travel, public engagement and advocacy, and was the first presidential spouse to hold regular press conferences and write a daily newspaper column. Her outspokenness, particularly on civil rights for African Americans, drew controversy early in her years in the [[White House]]. After her husband's death in 1945, she served as a U.S. delegate to the United Nations General Assembly and was the first chair of the UN Commission on Human Rights. She took a leading role in designing the text of the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]] and in gaining international support for it; it was adopted in 1948. [[Harry S. Truman]] called her the "First Lady of the World." She later chaired the Presidential Commission on the Status of Women under President [[John F. Kennedy]].

Duchess of Aquitaine (1137–1204), queen of France (1137–52) and queen of England (1154–89). Heiress of the House of Poitiers, which controlled much of southwestern France, she ruled Aquitaine jointly with her husbands and with two of her sons, Richard I and John. Her marriage to Louis VII of France was annulled in 1152 on grounds of [[Consanguinity|consanguinity]]. She then married Henry, Duke of Normandy, who became [[Henry II of England|Henry II]] in 1154. The couple had five sons and three daughters, but they became estranged, and Henry imprisoned her for supporting a 1173 revolt by their sons. She was released in 1189 and acted as regent during Richard's absences from England and France. After Richard's death in 1199, she campaigned successfully for John's succession. Many of the surviving accounts are chronicles written by clerics associated with royal courts, and later writers created both a "Black Legend" and an opposing "Golden Myth" of a feminist heroine.

Group decision-making process in which a population or group votes to choose individuals for public office or other positions of responsibility. Elections have been the usual mechanism of [[Democracy|representative democracy]] since the 17th century, and are also used by clubs, [[Voluntary association|voluntary associations]], [[Corporation|corporations]] and other organizations. Elections were used in [[Ancient Greece]] and [[Ancient Rome]], and in the medieval period to select rulers such as the Holy Roman Emperor and the [[Pope|pope]]. In [[Athens]], the democratic archetype, elections were considered an oligarchic institution, and most offices were filled by allotment, or sortition, in which office holders were chosen by lot. The earliest recorded popular elections of officials, for the ephors of [[Sparta]] in 754 BC, made all citizens eligible to vote and hold office. Electoral reform seeks fairer electoral systems, and psephology studies election results.

English rock band. Formed in [[Birmingham]] in 1970 by Jeff Lynne, Roy Wood and drummer Bev Bevan, the group blended pop and classical arrangements, and its name puns on electric light and light orchestral music. After Wood left in 1972, Lynne became the sole leader. Its most commercially successful album was the double album *Out of the Blue* (1977), and *Discovery* (1979) and *Time* (1981) reached the top of the British charts. The band sold over 50 million records worldwide. Four key members were inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2017.

Specialized chair used for execution by electrocution. Alfred P. Southwick, a dentist in [[Buffalo, New York]], conceived the method in 1881 as a more humane alternative to [[Hanging|hanging]]. It was first used in 1890 and became a common method of capital punishment in the United States and the [[Philippines]]. Its use declined with the adoption of [[Lethal injection|lethal injection]], although electrocution remains legal in several U.S. states.

Physical property of [[Matter|matter]] that causes it to experience a force in an electromagnetic field. Charge is positive or negative: like charges repel and unlike charges attract. In ordinary matter, negative charge is carried by [[Electron|electrons]] and positive charge by the [[Proton|protons]] in atomic nuclei. Charge is quantized in integer multiples of the elementary charge, about 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C, and in an isolated system the total charge does not change. Electric charges produce [[Electric field|electric fields]], and their interaction with the electromagnetic field is the source of the electromagnetic force. [[Coulomb's law]] makes that force proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The SI unit is the [[Coulomb|coulomb]] (C). [[Michael Faraday]] was the first to note the discrete nature of charge, in his electrolysis experiments, and [[Robert Millikan]]'s oil drop experiment measured the elementary charge.

Flow of charged particles, such as electrons or [[Ion|ions]], through a conductor or space. It is defined as the net rate at which [[Electric charge|electric charge]] flows through a surface. In wires the charge carriers are usually electrons, in [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]] they can be electrons or holes, and in electrolytes they are ions. The SI unit is the [[Ampere|ampere]] (A), equal to one [[Coulomb|coulomb]] per second. Currents create [[Magnetic field|magnetic fields]] used in motors, generators, inductors and transformers. In ordinary conductors they cause Joule heating, which produces light in [[Incandescent light bulb|incandescent bulbs]]. By convention, current runs in the direction of positive charge, opposite to electron flow in wires.

Genus of freshwater fish native to South America, *Electrophorus*, whose members stun prey with shocks of up to 860 volts. The electrical abilities of the fish were first studied in 1775, contributing to the invention of the [[Electric battery|electric battery]] in 1800. Despite the name, electric eels are not closely related to [[Eel|true eels]] but belong to the order Gymnotiformes. They are nocturnal, obligate air-breathers that mainly eat fish, and they keep growing throughout life. Captive specimens have lived for over 20 years. In 2019 the genus was divided into three species: *E. electricus*, *E. voltai* and *E. varii*.

Physical field that surrounds [[Electric charge|electrically charged]] particles and exerts attractive or repulsive forces on other charges. Two charges must be present for these forces to act. The force follows [[Coulomb's law]], growing with the magnitude of the charges and weakening with distance. Defined as the force per unit charge on a positive test charge at rest, the field is measured in volts per meter (V/m), equal to newtons per coulomb (N/C). Electric fields originate from electric charges and time-varying currents, and together with magnetic fields they form the [[Electromagnetic field|electromagnetic field]]. In atoms, the field between the [[Atomic nucleus|nucleus]] and electrons holds them together, and the interaction between atoms gives rise to [[Chemical bond|chemical bonding]]. [[Michael Faraday]] introduced field lines to visualize the field.

Electromechanical device that converts mechanical energy to electrical energy for use in an external circuit. Sources of mechanical energy include [[Steam turbine|steam turbines]], gas turbines, water turbines, [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engines]], [[Wind turbine|wind turbines]] and even hand cranks. Generators produce nearly all the electric power for worldwide [[Electrical grid|grids]]. Dynamos generate pulsing direct current through a commutator, while alternators generate [[Alternating current|alternating current]]. The principle of electromagnetic induction, later called [[Faraday's law of induction]], was discovered by [[Michael Faraday]] in 1831–1832, and his Faraday disk, invented in 1831, was the first electromagnetic generator. Motors and generators are very similar, and some [[Electric motor|motors]] can run in reverse as generators.

Guitar that requires electric amplification to be heard at typical performance volumes. Pickups convert string vibrations into electrical signals, which [[Loudspeaker|loudspeakers]] reproduce, and effects such as reverb, distortion and overdrive shape the sound. Jazz guitarists adopted the instrument, which allowed single-note solos in big bands. Early models were hollow-bodied, and solid-body designs such as Leo Fender's Telecaster (1950) and Stratocaster (1954) followed. During the 1950s and 1960s the electric guitar became the most important instrument in popular music, central to [[Blues|electric blues]], [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]] and [[Heavy metal music|heavy metal]]. In rock, it serves as a rhythm instrument playing chords and riffs, or as a lead instrument for melodies and solos.

Device that produces light from electricity, the most common form of artificial lighting. The three main categories are [[Incandescent light bulb|incandescent lamps]], in which a filament is heated white-hot by current; gas-discharge lamps, such as fluorescent lamps; and [[Light-emitting diode|light-emitting diodes]] (LEDs), which emit light as electrons cross a band gap in a [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]]. In 1802 Vasily Petrov developed the first persistent electric arc, and [[Humphry Davy]] demonstrated an arc light in 1806. [[Thomas Edison]] and Joseph Swan independently developed functional incandescent lamps in the late 1870s and 1880s. William D. Coolidge introduced a [[Tungsten|tungsten]] filament, for which he applied for a patent in 1912, and it became standard. Energy efficiency has significantly improved since the 19th century.

Electric potential energy per unit charge at a point in an [[Electric field|electric field]], also called electrostatic potential. It is measured in joules per [[Coulomb|coulomb]], or [[Volt|volts]] (V), and is often denoted V or φ. It is the [[Work (physics)|work]] needed to move a test charge from a reference point to a specific point in a static field, normalized to unit charge. The reference point is conventionally the Earth or a point at infinity, where the potential is zero. The potential difference between two points is the work done per unit charge when a charge moves between them. In classical electrostatics the field is the gradient of the potential. In time-varying fields, the potential combines with the magnetic vector potential to describe the field.

Final stage in the delivery of electricity, from the transmission system to individual consumers. Distribution substations lower transmission voltage to medium voltage, usually between 600 V and 35 kV, using [[Transformer|transformers]]. Primary distribution lines carry this power to distribution transformers near customers, which step it down to the utilization voltage used by lighting and appliances; in the United States, residential customers usually receive 120/240 V. Urban distribution is mainly underground, while rural distribution is mostly overhead on utility poles. Distribution became necessary in the 1880s, when electricity began to be generated at [[Power station|power stations]] rather than where it was used. Substations use [[Circuit breaker|circuit breakers]] and switches to disconnect parts of the network.

Bulk movement of electrical energy from a generating site, such as a power plant, to an electrical substation, carried by transmission lines. Lines carry either [[Alternating current|alternating current]] (AC) or [[Direct current|direct current]] (DC). Voltage is raised for long-distance transmission and reduced for local distribution, because higher voltages mean lower currents and lower losses. Most North American lines are three-phase AC, while high-voltage direct current (HVDC) is used for long distances, submarine cables and links between grids that are not synchronized. Underground transmission costs more to install but lowers maintenance costs. Interconnected lines form networks that offer redundant routes; the U.S. Northeast experienced blackouts in 1965, 1977 and 2003. The combined transmission and distribution network is known as the [[Electrical grid|electrical grid]].

Order of flattened cartilaginous fishes with enlarged pectoral fins, able to produce electric discharges. Its 69 species in four families discharge 8 to 220 [[Volt|volts]] to stun prey and deter predators. The fish lie in wait below sand and use shocks to capture invertebrates and small fish. The undersea torpedo weapon is named after the genus [[Torpedo]], whose name comes from Latin *torpere*, meaning "to be stiffened or paralyzed." The ancient Greeks used the rays to numb pain during childbirth and operations. The electric organs were studied in the 1770s, and [[Henry Cavendish]] built an artificial ray of Leyden jars in 1773 to mimic their behavior. Their research is thought to have influenced [[Luigi Galvani]] and [[Alessandro Volta]], founders of electrophysiology and electrochemistry.

Assembly of one or more [[Wire|wires]], running side by side or bundled, that carries [[Electric current|electric current]]. Cables connect two or more devices, transferring power or electrical signals, and undersea cables carry long-distance communication. Conductors are usually insulated and may be stranded for flexibility. Copper wires are often plated with [[Tin|tin]], gold or silver, which resist oxidation and ease soldering. Insulation was once made of cloth, rubber or paper, but plastics are used today except in high-reliability power cables. [[Polyethylene]], invented in 1930, is still a very common insulation material, though it was not available outside military use until after World War II. Any current-carrying cable radiates an [[Electromagnetic field|electromagnetic field]] and can pick up noise from other fields, which is usually undesirable.

Electromechanical device that creates an electrical connection between parts of a circuit, or between different circuits. Connections may be removable, require a tool, or be permanent. The male component, or plug, joins the female component, or socket. Thousands of configurations serve power, data and audiovisual applications, classed as inline or cable connectors, chassis or panel connectors, [[Printed circuit board|PCB]]-mount connectors, and splice or butt connectors. In computing, connectors form part of the physical layer of the OSI model. Copper alloy electrodes are often coated with [[Gold|gold]], [[Nickel|nickel]] or [[Tin|tin]] to resist [[Corrosion|corrosion]] and reduce contact resistance. Contact carriers are usually plastic, which is insulating.

Interconnected network for delivering electricity from producers to consumers. Grids consist of [[Power station|power stations]], substations that step [[Voltage|voltage]] up or down, [[Electric power transmission|transmission]] lines over long distances, and [[Electric power distribution|distribution]] networks to customers. Power stations are typically built close to energy sources and far from densely populated areas. Grids are nearly always synchronous, with three-phase [[Alternating current|alternating current]] frequencies synchronized. Grids range from microgrids, which can disconnect and operate autonomously during outages, to wide-area synchronous grids covering whole countries or continents. North America has four major interconnections, and most of continental Europe is served by one grid. About 840 million people, mostly in Africa, had no access to grid electricity in 2017, down from 1.2 billion in 2010.

Opposition of a circuit to [[Alternating current|alternating current]], combining resistance and reactance. Impedance is a complex quantity, usually denoted Z and measured in [[Ohm|ohms]] (Ω), the same unit as resistance. It is the ratio of the complex voltage across a two-terminal element to the complex current through it, and it generally depends on the frequency of the sinusoidal voltage. Resistance forms the real part of impedance, while reactance, arising from [[Inductance|inductance]] and [[Capacitance|capacitance]], forms the imaginary part. Impedance allows AC networks to be analyzed with a linear law, and its reciprocal, admittance, is measured in [[Siemens (unit)|siemens]]. The term was coined by Oliver Heaviside in July 1886.
